transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, hi, doc. Thanks for seeing me. It’s kind of a long story, but to try and boil it down... well, what brings me in is this feeling I get. It's honestly like I’ve got a motor humming right under my skin. Just this constant, vibrating energy, especially whenever I’m supposed to just sit still and listen. 

I work as a building cleaner, a janitor over at the community college, and usually, that's fine because I'm on my feet, moving around, buffing floors, emptying bins, keeping busy. I've got my associate's degree, but I like the physical work because I get to move. But they have these mandatory staff meetings every Tuesday morning, and I swear, the minute my rear end hits that chair, my legs start bouncing. It’s like this physical pressure building up inside me. 

And it's not just work, either. Same thing happens on Sundays. I volunteer with the events team at my church, and we have these briefings before the service to go over the schedule and who is setting up what. Everyone else is just sitting there calmly, drinking their coffee, listening to the coordinator, and I’m just... I can't do it. I end up shifting my weight constantly, crossing and uncrossing my legs, tapping my boots, and eventually, I just have to stand up and pace in the back of the room. Or I’ll find some ridiculous excuse to move around, like I'll pretend I need to check the thermostat, or I'll go inspect a lightbulb that's been flickering, or I'll go get my fourth cup of water just to have a reason to walk down the hall. I just can't sit there. It's driving me crazy, and it's starting to make other people look at me like I'm not paying attention or I'm trying to be disruptive, which isn't it at all, I just have to move.
Do you feel this same restlessness or need to move even when you’re not sitting, like when you’re standing in line or trying to lie down to sleep?

Well, standing in line... you know, it's funny you ask about that because just the other day I was at the DMV. Now, usually, I try to avoid the DMV like the plague, right? I renew my truck's registration online whenever I can, but this time I had to go in person because of some issue with my address not updating in their system after I moved apartments last year. So I'm standing there in this line that's practically wrapping around the building, and honestly... no, I didn't really feel that same motor running. 

I mean, sure, I was shifting my weight a bit, maybe leaning on the wall, but because I'm already on my feet, it's just... different. I can stretch my calves, I can take a half-step forward, I can look around. It's not that trapped feeling I get when I'm stuck in a chair. Even at the grocery store—I usually go to the one down on 4th street, mostly on Thursday nights when it's less crowded—if I get stuck behind someone with a million coupons, I'm generally fine. I can look at the magazines, I can tap my foot, but it doesn't build up into that crazy pressure where I feel like I'm going to explode.

And as for sleeping... gosh, my sleep routine is a whole other story. I usually get home, take a really hot shower to wash off the floor wax smell—you wouldn't believe how that stuff clings to your clothes, even through the heavy work shirts we have to wear—and by the time my head hits the mattress, I'm pretty wiped out physically. I don't really lay there feeling like I need to get up and jog. I might toss and turn a little bit just to get my shoulder comfortable, because I've got this old rotator cuff thing from running the heavy floor buffers for so many years, but it's not that vibrating energy I was telling you about with the staff meetings. It really just seems to be when I'm forced to park my rear end in a chair and be a captive audience, you know? So, yeah, I guess I haven't really noticed it when I'm standing or lying down.

When you're in situations that require focus—like reading instructions, following a conversation, or watching a movie—do you find yourself getting easily distracted, losing track of what you're doing, or acting on impulse without thinking it through?

Well, honestly... no, not really. I mean, focus isn't exactly my problem. It's more about the sitting still part. Like with reading instructions... I fix things all the time. Just last week, one of the big commercial vacuums at the college—the heavy-duty ones with the extra-long cords that we use for the main lecture halls—it completely broke down. The brush roll just stopped spinning. Now, we have a maintenance guy, Jerry, but he was out sick with some stomach bug, so I decided to take a look at it myself. I pulled up the manual on my phone, and I sat there on the floor of the supply closet for a good forty-five minutes, reading through the schematics, figuring out how to take the casing apart without snapping the plastic tabs, and I got it fixed. I didn't lose track of what I was doing at all. I was totally zeroed in on it. 

And conversations? I'm fine with conversations. Especially if I'm moving while I'm talking. Like when I'm working with my buddy Dave on the night shift, we'll talk for hours about football, or his kids, or whatever, while we're emptying trash cans and wiping down the whiteboards. I follow exactly what he's saying. I don't zone out or anything. Even if I'm just standing there talking to the pastor at church after service, I'm listening. I might be shifting my weight, like I said, but I'm hearing every word. 

And movies... well, I don't go to the theater much anymore because the seats are so uncomfortable and, again, I hate being trapped in a chair. But at home? I'll put on an old Western—I love those old Clint Eastwood movies, they just don't make them like that anymore, you know? The pacing is so different from the stuff they put out now with all the CGI explosions. Anyway, I'll put one on, and I'll watch the whole thing. Now, I might be folding laundry while I watch it, or maybe I'm fixing a broken hinge on a cabinet door, or just pacing around the living room during the slow parts, but I'm paying attention. I know exactly what the plot is. I'm not getting distracted by a squirrel out the window or forgetting what I'm doing. 

And as for acting on impulse... no, I don't think so. I'm a pretty methodical guy, honestly. You kind of have to be when you're cleaning a building that size. You have a routine, you have a set order of operations, and you stick to it, otherwise, you miss things and people complain. I don't just randomly decide to do something crazy without thinking it through. My problem really is just that physical pressure, that motor running when I have to sit down and be quiet. The focus part? My brain works just fine as long as my body is allowed to do its thing.
